Called by Committee Chair

  SPECIAL – BUDGET AND FINANCE ADVISORY COMMITTEE (BFAC) MEETING

  Friday, July 10, 2026

  ROOM 401, CITY HALL - 1:00 PM
  200 NORTH SPRING STREET, LOS ANGELES, CA 90012

  MEMBERS:  RON S. GALPERIN, CHAIR
  DERRIC J. JOHNSON, VICE CHAIR
  GILDA HAAS
  JOSEPH M. LUMARDA
  TOM DE SIMONE

  Armando Bencomo - Legislative Assistant - (213) 978-1080
  (or Clerk.BudgetandFinanceCommittee@lacity.org)

  Submit written comment at LACouncilComment.com

The audio for Committee meetings is broadcast live on the internet at https://clerk.lacity.gov/calendar.

The Committee will take public comment from members of the public in-person only; there will be no public comment by
teleconference. Additional information regarding Committee procedures provided at the end of this agenda.

For interpretation services and Sign Language Interpreters, at no cost, please contact clerk.interpretation@lacity.org or call (213)
978-1133 and provide the language desired, specific meeting, meeting date, and the number of people in the group.

All requests should be submitted with as much advance notice as possible, preferably two business days prior to the meeting you
wish to attend for additional language interpretation and five business days for Sign Language Interpretation. We will do our best to
accommodate requests with shorter notice, but securing last-minute interpreters or captioners may not always be feasible.

ITEM(S)

 (1)  Call to Order and Roll Call
  (2)  Public Comment

  • Multiple Agenda Item Comment
  • General Public Comment

 (3)  Approval of Minutes
  The Committee will review and approve the Minutes of the May 1,
  2026, Budget and Finance Advisory Committee meeting.

 (4)  Staff Update
  Staff will share recent stakeholder engagement efforts and relevant
  City-wide policies.

 (5)  Office of the City Administrative Officer (CAO) Presentation
  Office of the CAO will present an overview of the City’s Adopted
  Budget Fiscal Year 2026-27 and fiscal outlook.

 (6)  Action Plan Discussion
  Committee members will discuss next steps regarding conversations
  and policy research needed to work towards final committee
  recommendations and final report.

 (7)  Open Discussion
  Committee members will refine the BFAC work plan, goals, and focus
  areas for the year, as needed.

 (8)  Next Steps and Calendar Review

 (9)  Adjournment

SUPPORTING MATERIALS

Materials relating to items on the agenda are available on the Budget and Finance Advisory Committee webpage found at
https://councilcommittee.lacity.gov/budget/BudgetandFinanceAdvisory/. To subscribe to the Budget and Finance Advisory Committee
agendas, please subscribe using this link: https://lacity.gov/government/subscribe-agendas/city-council

PUBLIC INPUT AT CITY COUNCIL COMMITTEE MEETINGS
 Members of the public who wish to speak on one or multiple items shall have an opportunity to speak up to one minute per item up
to a total of two minutes for two or more agenda items. At regular meetings, members of the public shall also have an opportunity to
speak up to one minute for general public comment on any matter within the subject-matter jurisdiction of the Committee. The
Committee is not required to take general public comment at special meetings. The Committee may limit the total amount of time for
public comment on any specific agenda item, on all agenda-items collectively, and/or on general public comment, based on the
anticipated time required to hear from public speakers on any given or all agenda items, on the availability of Committee members
and the need to maintain quorum, and on any other relevant factor. The Committee shall not discuss or take action relative to any
general public comment except as explicitly permitted under the Brown Act.

COMMITTEE INFORMATION, ASSIGNMENTS, AND STRUCTURE

https://clerk.lacity.gov/clerk-services/cps/council-committee-meetings/info-assignments-structure

SPECIAL ACCOMMODATION

Requests for reasonable modification or accommodation from individuals with disabilities, consistent with the Americans with
Disabilities Act, can be made by contacting the City Clerk's Office at (213) 978-1133. For Telecommunications Relay Service for the
hearing impaired, please see the information below.

NOTICE TO PAID REPRESENTATIVES

If a member of the public is compensated to monitor, attend, or speak at this meeting, City law may require them to register as a
lobbyist and report this activity. More information can be found at Los Angeles Municipal Code 48.01 et seq. or at
ethics.lacity.org/lobbying. Further assistance can be found by contacting the Ethics Commission at (213) 978-1960 or
ethics.commission@lacity.org.

EXHAUSTION OF ADMINISTRATIVE REMEDIES

A member of the public seeking to challenge a City action in court may be limited to raising only those issues raised at the public
hearing described in this notice, or in written correspondence delivered to the City Clerk prior to the public hearing in time reasonably
to be considered by the Committee members. Any written correspondence delivered to the City Clerk before the City Council's final
action on a matter will become a part of the administrative record.

TELECOMMUNICATIONS RELAY SERVICE (TRS) COMMUNICATIONS

Telephone communication is one of the most important forms of communication in society today. Due to advancements in
technology, telephone devices have evolved with new services and capabilities. Individuals who are deaf and hard of hearing, and
individuals with a speech disability, may be able to avail themselves of both for peer-to-peer and third-party telecommunications
relay service (TRS) communications. Telecommunications Relay Service is a telephone service that allows persons with hearing or
speech disabilities to place and receive telephone calls. TRS is available in all 50 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico and
the U.S. territories for local and/or long distance calls. TRS providers - generally telephone companies - are compensated for the
costs of providing TRS from either a state or a federal fund. There is no cost to the TRS user.

What forms of TRS are available? There are several forms of TRS, depending on the particular needs of the user and the equipment
available: TRS includes: Text to Voice TIY-Based TRS; Speech-to-Speech Relay Service; Shared Non-English Language Relay
Service; Captioned Telephone Relay Service; Internet Protocol Relay Service; and Video Relay Service. Please visit this site for
detail descriptions, https://www.fcc.gov/consumers/guides/telecommunications-relay-service-trs.

Don't hang up! Some people hang up on TRS calls because they think the caller is a telemarketer. If you hear, "Hello, this is the
relay service…" when you pick up the phone, please don't hang up! You are about to talk, through a TRS provider, to a person who
is deaf, hard-of-hearing, or has a speech disability.

For more information about FCC programs to promote access to telecommunications services for people with disabilities, visit the
FCC's Disability Rights Office website.

JOURNAL – SPECIAL BUDGET AND FINANCE ADVISORY COMMITTEE (BFAC) MEETING

  Friday, July 10, 2026

  ROOM 401, CITY HALL - 1:00 PM
  200 NORTH SPRING STREET, LOS ANGELES, CA 90012

  MEMBERS:  RON S. GALPERIN, CHAIR
  DERRIC J. JOHNSON, VICE CHAIR
  GILDA HAAS
  JOSEPH M. LUMARDA
  TOM DE SIMONE

  Armando Bencomo - Legislative Assistant - (213) 978-1080
  (or Clerk.BudgetandFinanceCommittee@lacity.org)

  Submit written comment at LACouncilComment.com

The audio for this meeting is broadcast live on the internet at https://clerk.lacity.gov/calendar. Additional information
regarding Committee procedures provided at the end of this agenda.

ITEM(S)

 (1)  Call to Order and Roll Call

  Members Present: Ron S. Galperin, Derric J. Johnson, Gilda Haas, Joseph M.
  Lumarda, Tom De Simone (5); Absent: (0)

  Chairperson Galperin called the meeting to order at 1:07 p.m.

 (2)  Public Comment

  • Multiple Agenda Item Comment
  • General Public Comment

  The Committee provided an opportunity for Multiple Agenda Item and General Public
  Comments.
 (3)  Approval of Minutes
  The Committee will review and approve the Minutes of the May 1,
  2026, Budget and Finance Advisory Committee meeting.

  Member Lumarda moved to approve the Minutes of the May 1, 2026 Budget and
  Finance Advisory Committee, which was seconded by Vice Chair Johnson – Ayes:
  Galperin, Johnson, Haas, Lumarda, De Simone (5); Nays: (0)

(4)  Staff Update
  Staff will share recent stakeholder engagement efforts and relevant
  City-wide policies.

  Charles Turner, Council District 5, provided a staff update on milestones as the
  Committee transitions from the research phase into the implementation phase for the
  development of recommendations to the Budget and Finance Committee, and
  introduced UCLA Luskin Leadership Fellows Shaine Stuhlmuller, Hannah Klubeck, and
  Alberto Espiricueta (BFAC staff). Staff updates will broadly center on the four key areas
  of external engagement, Council and legislative updates, staff recommendations, and
  general Committee calendar review. The first BFAC Progress Report dated June 26,
  2026 has been published and is available for public review in Council File No. 25-0314.

  Regarding external engagement, BFAC staff has continued to highlight the Committee’s
  progress to garner broader engagement through individual meetings and ad hoc
  subcommittee meetings. BFAC staff has increased engagement with staff from all 15
  Council District Offices, and will be developing a strategic engagement plan to involve
  external stakeholders, such as community-based organizations, think tanks, etc. BFAC
  staff has also met with Justin Ramirez, Executive Director of the Charter Reform
  Commission, to solicit advice relative to committee advancement.

  Regarding Council and legislative updates, BFAC staff anticipates to align and build
  upon efforts already underway within the City, including the efforts of the Charter Reform
  Commission and ongoing research memos and report-backs directed by the City Council
  that are already available as public data. The Charter Reform Commission transmitted
  its final report with recommendations to the City Council on April 2, 2026, which is
  available in Council File No. 26-0489. The City Council adopted a subset of the Charter
  Reform Commission’s recommendations that will move forward for placement on the
  November 2026 election ballot, while other recommendations were recommended for
  further study. Certain recommendations align with the Committee’s focus areas that have
  been discussed, which will be highlighted by BFAC staff for discussion and potential
  action. City Council Meetings will resume after the Summer Recess starting on Tuesday,
  August 4, 2026.
   Staff recommendations for this month involve a high-level review of the Charter Reform
  Commission’s recommendations that overlap with the Committee’s focus areas, such as
  liability insurance and the City’s ability to generate revenue through commercial
  activities. BFAC staff recommends a closer evaluation of the overlapping
  recommendations to ensure the Committee’s potential recommendations in the
  overlapping areas are complementary rather than being duplicative. They also
  recommend further exploration of other relevant Charter Reform recommendations that
  were approved and tabled by the City Council. BFAC staff will share additional
  information with the respective ad hoc subcommittees.

  Regarding Committee calendar review, the next regular BFAC Meeting is scheduled on
  Friday, August 7, 2026 at 1:00 p.m. A Special BFAC Meeting will be scheduled thereafter
  on Friday, September 11, 2026 at 1:00 p.m.

(5)  Office of the City Administrative Officer (CAO) Presentation
  Office of the CAO will present an overview of the City’s Adopted
  Budget Fiscal Year 2026-27 and fiscal outlook.

  Benjamin Ceja, Assistant City Administrative Officer (CAO), presented an overview of the
  revenue estimates for the City’s Fiscal Year (FY) 2026-27 Adopted Budget in comparison
  with the FY 2025-26 Adopted Budget and the FY 2025-26 Revised Budget, authorized
  City staffing levels of regular positions over a 20-year period, status of the Reserve
  Fund, four-year outlooks and key assumptions for revenues and expenditures,
  compliance with the City’s Financial Policies, and future initiatives to achieve budgetary
  structural balance. The revenue estimates for FY 2026-27 incorporated increased
  revenue from business taxes and tax discovery efforts undertaken by the Office of
  Finance, increases in the Utility Users Tax and Sales Tax revenue, and increased
  parking fine revenue attributed to automated bus lane enforcement receipts. Fluctuations
  in authorized staffing levels over a 20-year period were a result of revenue shortfalls and
  austerity measures that were offered to civilian employees as the Early Retirement
  Incentive Program during the Great Recession, and the Separation Incentive Program
  during the COVID-19 pandemic.

  The CAO’s Office issued $1.4 billion in Tax and Revenue Anticipation Notes (TRAN) with
  a 2.75 percent yield to cover cash flow for pension payments paid by July 15, 2026, as
  General Fund revenue is received later in the Fiscal Year. A discount is provided to the
  City for an upfront pension payment that is invested by the respective pension fund to
  earn a rate of return based on the cash on hand. Property tax revenue, which is the
  highest source of revenue, will be distributed in two installments during December 2026
  and April 2027. The key assumptions for the four-year outlook include no recession and
  a return to the historic level of revenue growth, no service restorations or expansions,
  and no new labor costs. Factors that may impact the four-year outlook include major
 expenses, labor negotiations, permit fee waivers, and potential Charter Reform
amendments. The four-year outlook for FY 2026-27, which factors in the Los Angeles
Convention Center Expansion and Modernization Project, demonstrates deficits in FY
2028-29 due to future debt service payments. The four-year outlook for a proposed
Department of Recreation and Parks’ (RAP) Allocation Increase incorporates a proposed
ten-year phase increase of the RAP’s General Fund allocation to 0.065 percent.

The FY 2026-27 Adopted Budget is in compliance with the City’s Financial Policies
relative to the Reserve Fund threshold requirement of at least five percent of all General
Fund revenues by starting with 6.01 percent of General Fund revenues, and the Budget
Stabilization Fund will start with a balance of $200 million. Debt service is 2.41 percent
under the six-percent threshold for non-voter approved direct debt, and at 3.71 percent
under the 15-percent threshold for voter and non-voter-approved direct. The debt service
is also in adherence to Municipal Improvement Corporation of Los Angeles (MICLA)
operating policies. The FY 2026-27 Adopted Budget is also in compliance with the
Financial Policy relative to one-time revenues being used for one-time expenditures.

The FY 2026-27 Adopted Budget is not in compliance with the Financial Policies relative
to Cumulative General Fund Reserves, Capital and Investments, and Structural Balance.
The Cumulative General Fund Reserves balance of 8.91 percent should be at least ten
percent of General Fund revenues. The FY 2026-27 Adopted Budget invests 1.3 percent
of the General Fund revenues toward Capital and Technology Investments, which should
be at least 1.5 percent of General Fund revenues. Expenditures are estimated to exceed
revenues by $166 million in FY 2027-28, which is not in compliance with the Structural
Balance Financial Policy. Initiatives to achieve structural balance include a strategic plan
for transitioning to a two-year budgeting process through a proposed Charter
amendment, dedicating resources in the CAO’s Office and City Attorney’s Office with six
months of funding starting in January 2027 to centralize liability mitigation and establish
departmental accountability, and the development of fiscal transparency protocols
associated with labor negotiations to document costs related to the negotiated labor
contract terms before decisions are made. A Charter Reform recommendation to
develop a five-year policy for a Capital Improvement Program would allow the City to
invest in this area as a Citywide strategic approach.

The Committee and Assistant CAO Ceja discussed the potential alignment of the two-
year budget cycle with schedules for labor agreement negotiations, the positions
allocated to liability mitigation initiatives, parking enforcement revenue and current roles
of full-time traffic officer positions, the TRAN rate in comparison to the treasury yield,
maximizing interfund borrowing, the proposed increased General Fund allocation to the
RAP, calculation and reporting mechanisms for personal business property taxes
collected by the County of Los Angeles (County) on behalf of the City, potential
increases to the Board of Police Commissioners fees, and automatic adjustments
incorporated into fee increases.
 (6)  Action Plan Discussion
  Committee members will discuss next steps regarding conversations
  and policy research needed to work towards final committee
  recommendations and final report.

  The Committee discussed the policy solutions outlined in Appendix B of the BFAC
  Progress Report No. 1 dated June 26, 2026, and the proposed BFAC Roadmap with
  milestones for the development of the Committee’s recommendations to the Budget and
  Finance Committee. Regarding the City Treasury Return on Investment policy solution,
  the Committee requested additional information and discussion on the investment
  strategies of the City’s pension funds, as well as research on achieved investment
  returns, legal mandates and restrictions, and any innovative approaches undertaken by
  treasuries of other governmental entities within the State of California. The Committee
  also requested a follow-up discussion with the City Treasurer on this focus area, and a
  discussion on legal issues involved in interfund borrowing with representatives of the
  City Attorney’s Office and CAO’s Office.

  Regarding the liability claim payments policy solution, the Committee discussed
  revisiting this focus area after implementation of the CAO’s Office initiative to dedicate
  staffing and six months of funding to support liability mitigation and departmental
  accountability. The respective ad hoc subcommittee held a meeting with representatives
  of the Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) to discuss the potential implementation of
  personal liability per sworn officer to offset costs that impact General Fund revenue, best
  practices or pilot projects that would benefit the City, options for settlement of cases prior
  to entering into litigation, and investment in Artificial Intelligence and upgraded
  technology. Other revenue-generating initiatives include potential investment in the
  Controller’s Office employee structure to increase auditing capabilities, incorporating
  predictive analytics for infrastructure maintenance, using GIS mapping technology to
  identify hot spots to prioritize street and sidewalk repairs, advocating for litigation caps
  through the State Legislative Agenda, evaluating the governmental entity culture and
  approach to reducing liability claims and litigation, and evaluating international social
  impact bonds or foundations as potential revenue streams to incentivize investments.
  The Committee requested information on the County’s policies and efforts in addressing
  risk mitigation, a presentation by insurance companies that represent municipal
  governments or counties in the liability insurance market, a presentation on the status of
  the City Attorney’s efforts to establish caps on liability claims, and a presentation or
  report with a comparative analysis of other cities’ liability claims with percentages related
  to budget, population, and number of officers.

  Regarding the Special Funds management policy solution, the Committee requested to
  revisit the discussion with the Controller’s Office regarding the identification of under-
  utilized funds or funds with revenue accumulation that have outpaced expenditures, and
  establishing a collaboration for a centralized and incremental approach for the utilization
  of such Special Funds while taking into consideration the applicable mandates and
   restrictions. The Committee also requested an analysis of prior City Controller
  recommendations regarding encumbrance policies that have not been fully implemented,
  and an expansive look at any Special Funds that can help fund a general purpose within
  an acceptable realm.

  Regarding the Real Asset Management policy solution, the respective ad hoc
  subcommittee has scheduled meetings to explore the topic of establishing a more
  comprehensive and organized approach for the highest and best use of City assets,
  such as establishing a system for the identification of City assets that could be used for
  revenue-generating site activities to magnify the value of the underlying property. The ad
  hoc subcommittee is also focusing on what was lost with the dissolution of the
  Community Redevelopment Agency of the City of Los Angeles (CRA/LA) that was
  beneficial in the real estate and financing markets, the limitations and legal constraints
  around redevelopment of City-owned land and alternative uses in light of the Surplus
  Land Act and housing prioritizations, and any potential economic opportunities based on
  locations and proximity to other properties with other uses. The Committee requested a
  discussion with former CRA/LA staff and land use attorneys with experience in public-
  private partnership developments regarding real estate management, financing, and any
  opportunities that may exist that would be beneficial to the City.

  Other focus areas to be explored and discussed at a later date include the creation of a
  Los Angeles Municipal Development Corporation, the annual Cost Allocation Plan (CAP)
  Calculation and Utilization policy for overhead compensation, leveraging of City-owned
  intellectual property, evaluating the calculation for personal business property tax
  revenue, fee restructuring, establishing commercial delivery fees, and parking
  enforcement revenue. The Committee requested the addition of potential dollar amounts
  to prioritize the revenue-generating opportunities, and allotment of time during each
  meeting to discuss the cost-savings and revenue-generating proposals and codify the
  actionable items with short-term, mid-term, and long-term implementation schedules.
  Two changes in the proposed BFAC Roadmap were noted to include the development of
  investment recommendations with TRAN recommendations, and updating the August 7,
  2026 BFAC Meeting date.

  Member Lumarda moved to approve the proposed BFAC Roadmap as discussed, which
  was seconded by Member De Simone – Ayes: Galperin, Johnson, Haas, Lumarda, De
  Simone (5): Nays: (0)

(7)  Open Discussion
  Committee members will refine the BFAC work plan, goals, and focus
  areas for the year, as needed.

  No discussion on this Item.
  (8)  Next Steps and Calendar Review

  The next BFAC Meeting is scheduled on Friday, August 7, 2026 at 1:00 p.m. in City Hall.

 (9)  Adjournment

  The Committee Meeting was adjourned at 3:15 p.m. with the following Members present:

  Present: Ron S. Galperin, Derric J. Johnson, Gilda Haas, Tom De Simone (4);
  Absent: Joseph M. Lumarda (1)
